Likely no gain or a loss; measure on your own eval before shipping, and consider expansions only for the first stage or for shifted domains
No effect either way
A gain only if N is at least 8
explain: Weller et al. found strong models are generally harmed: MonoT5-3B lost 4.0 on DL19 and 14.7 on FiQA. Expansion tends to help weaker models or large format shifts, so it must be evaluated, not assumed.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: The Purdue model: levels from field devices to the enterprise
question: Why does NIST say outbound rules from the control network should be as strict as inbound ones?
options: Because outbound traffic is always faster
Because PLCs send too many emails
Because an infected control-network machine that can reach the internet or enterprise freely gives attackers a channel out and a path back in
Because inbound rules do not work in OT
explain: Malware on a Level 2 or 3 host needs to talk to its operator. Strict egress filtering blocks that and limits what a compromised host can reach. NIST calls unmanaged outbound connections 'a significant risk'.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Stuxnet, the controller that lied
question: An engineer uploads the PLC program through the plant's engineering workstation and it matches the approved version exactly. Why might that not be enough after a Stuxnet-style infection?
options: The workstation's PLC communication library may be intercepted, so the tool shows a cleaned view while the PLC runs extra code
Uploads are always encrypted
PLCs cannot store more than one program
Hashes cannot be computed for PLC code
explain: Stuxnet's fake s7otbxdx.dll hid its blocks from Step 7 reads. Verification must use a trusted path: a clean machine, vendor integrity features, or physical inspection of behaviour.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
question: A plant wants dashboards in the head office showing live tank levels, and wants no possible inbound path. Which design fits?
options: A unidirectional gateway pushing historian data to a replica in the DMZ, read by the head office
A firewall rule allowing the head office to query the PLCs
A VPN from head office into the control zone
Putting the PLCs on the internet behind a password
explain: A data diode is physically one-way, so the replica can be fed without any route back into OT. Firewalls and VPNs can be misconfigured to allow inbound traffic; a diode cannot.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
question: In federation, what does the service provider actually verify when Ana arrives?
options: Ana's password, forwarded by the IdP
That Ana's browser has an IdP cookie
A signed statement from the IdP, checked with the IdP's public key it stored in advance
Ana's MFA code, relayed by the browser
explain: NIST's definition: the RP does not verify the subscriber's authenticators. It verifies the IdP's signed assertion with a key from the trust agreement, and the IdP's own cookie belongs to the IdP's domain, which the app cannot read.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Validating a SAML response: every check, and the replay cache
question: The SP runs on three servers behind a load balancer, each with its own in-memory replay cache. What is the weakness?
options: None
The caches will overflow
An attacker can replay a captured assertion to a server that has not seen it yet
The IdP cannot sign for three servers
explain: A replay cache only works if every server that can accept the assertion consults it. Use a shared store with entries that expire at the assertion's NotOnOrAfter.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
question: During a planned rollover, why does the IdP publish the new key in metadata days before signing with it?
options: To give attackers less time
Because certificates take days to issue
So every SP has refreshed its metadata and trusts the new key before the first assertion signed with it arrives
To keep the metadata file small
explain: SPs refresh metadata on their own schedules. Publishing first and switching later means no SP ever receives an assertion signed with a key it does not know, so logins do not break.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: IdP compromise and Golden SAML: forging the whole federation
question: In the 2023 attacks Okta described, how did attackers impersonate users without stealing a signing key?
options: By cracking password hashes
By wrapping XML signatures
By using Super Administrator access to add a second IdP they controlled, whose assertions the org trusted
By replaying old assertions
explain: Okta reported a second IdP configured as an "impersonation app" through inbound federation, with usernames manipulated to match real users. Changing the trust configuration is as powerful as stealing a key, which is why IdP creation events deserve alerts.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
question: In the script, Ben's db:admin grant was approved by Ben. Why is that a finding even though a request exists?
options: Because database access should never be requested
Because a request without a ticket number is invalid
Because the person who benefits approved it, so no second person ever judged the need
Because admin rights can only be granted by HR
explain: An approval is a second person's judgment. When the requester approves their own request, the record looks complete but no independent check happened. This is the core of separation of duties (lesson 6).

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Role mining and role engineering: from a pile of grants to roles
question: A mined role for the support team includes the permission to delete customer accounts, because most support staff happen to hold it today. What should happen before the role is adopted?
options: Adopt it: mining reflects what people use
Remove the support team from RBAC entirely
The role owner checks each permission against the job; holding something widely is not evidence it is needed
Split the role so each person has a personal role
explain: Mining reproduces current access, including widespread over-provisioning. An owner must validate the role. Personal roles would recreate the original mess.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Bastions, jump hosts and session brokering
question: A company adds a jump server and requires all admin RDP to pass through it. Admins type their domain admin passwords into RDP sessions launched from the jump server. What has the company created?
options: A host where every admin credential passes through, which attackers will target with credential-theft tools
A complete privileged access solution
A network that no longer needs patching
A way to make domain admin passwords expire
explain: Microsoft's guidance warns exactly about this: jump servers where many sensitive sessions pass let attackers steal and reuse credentials. Keep secrets off the intermediary and protect it as a privileged system.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Measuring identity hygiene, detecting abuse, and running the programme
question: A role assignment granting database admin appears in the logs with no matching access request or JIT activation. What is the best reading and response?
options: It is normal background activity; ignore it
It is a performance problem in the governance tool
Wait for the next quarterly review
An out-of-process grant (ATT&CK T1098, Account Manipulation): investigate who made it and why, remove it if unexplained, and check what the account did
explain: Every grant should trace to a rule or request (lesson 1). A privileged grant outside the process is either a broken process or an attacker establishing access, and both need action now, not next quarter.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
question: A bridge inspection system must detect new cracks that appear as lines 1 to 2 pixels wide. The current pipeline uses opening with a 5x5 kernel. What happens?
options: Cracks are kept because opening only removes isolated single pixels
Cracks are erased, because opening removes structures that cannot contain the kernel
Cracks are thickened to 5 pixels
Opening has no effect on binary masks
explain: Erosion with a 5x5 kernel removes any structure narrower than 5 pixels, and dilation cannot restore what erosion deleted. The kernel must be smaller than the thinnest change to keep, or use an operation that matches the expected shape (for example a line-shaped kernel), accepting more noise.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Preparation: plan, people, contacts, retainers and logs
question: Your EDR keeps 30 days of telemetry and your SIEM 14 days. A partner reports that your credentials were sold on a forum six weeks ago. What is the consequence?
options: The earliest attacker activity is probably no longer in any log, so scoping will rely on disk and memory artefacts and the partner's information
None, because the EDR can still see the attacker
You can recover the old telemetry from the EDR vendor in all cases
You must restore the SIEM from backup
explain: Six weeks is about 42 days, longer than either retention window. Whatever happened at the start has aged out; forensic artefacts on disk (which persist longer) and external information become the main sources.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Hashing evidence and keeping a chain of custody
question: Why does RFC 3227 tell you to analyse a copy of your evidence copy?
options: Analysis tools usually require two copies
To save disk space
Analysis can change the data (for example file access times), and the evidence copy must stay as acquired
Because the first copy is always corrupted
explain: Opening and searching files changes metadata such as access times. Working on a second copy keeps the evidence copy, and its hash, exactly as acquired.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Memory forensics: processes, connections and injected code
question: Why might malware hidden by process injection survive a disk-only investigation?
options: Injected code always deletes the disk
Disk images cannot contain executables
The malicious code may live only in another process's memory, with no file on disk to scan
Injection only works on Linux
explain: With injection the malicious logic runs inside a legitimate process's memory and may never be written to disk. Only memory analysis (malfind-style checks, then extraction and scanning) sees it.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
question: When does the GDPR Article 33 clock for notifying the supervisory authority start?
options: When the controller becomes aware of the personal data breach
When the investigation is complete
When the first customer complains
When the attacker publishes the data
explain: Article 33 says not later than 72 hours after having become aware of the breach, where feasible. Information that is not yet available may be provided in phases.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: SQL from zero: tables, queries, quotes and comments
question: How does SQL read `WHERE username = 'ana' AND password = 'x' OR role = 'user'`?
options: username = 'ana' AND (password = 'x' OR role = 'user')
Left to right with no precedence
(username = 'ana' AND password = 'x') OR role = 'user'
It is a syntax error without parentheses
explain: AND binds tighter than OR, so the two AND-ed comparisons form one group and OR joins that group with role = 'user'. Every row with role user matches, whatever its username and password. Remember this for the next lesson.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
question: Why does OWASP prefer parameterised queries over correct escaping?
options: Escaping is slower
Parameterised queries encrypt the data
Escaping is not supported by modern databases
Escaping depends on context, dialect and configuration and must be done at every call site, while parameters keep values out of the SQL text entirely
explain: Correct escaping requires the right rules for the right context and database settings at every single call site. Parameters remove the problem: the SQL text is a constant and values never pass through the parser.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: NoSQL injection: when a value turns into an operator
question: Which single change most directly prevents operator injection in that login handler?
options: Escaping quotes in the password
Using HTTPS
Rejecting the request unless username and password are both plain strings
Renaming the password field
explain: The attack changes the value's type, not its characters, so escaping does nothing. A strict type check (or schema validation) ensures only plain strings reach the query.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: LDAP, XPath, header and log injection
question: Why does writing logs as JSON defeat log injection with newlines?
options: JSON forbids newlines in usernames
JSON logs are encrypted
Log readers ignore JSON files
The newline inside a value is encoded as the two characters backslash and n, so it cannot start a new record
explain: In JSON, a string value cannot contain a raw newline; the serializer writes it as an escape sequence. Each event stays one record, and the attacker's text is visible as data inside a field.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
question: A helper function declares `char buf[4096]` locally, prepares an `IORING_OP_READ` into it, calls `io_uring_submit`, and returns. The caller later waits for the CQE. What happens?
options: Safe: the kernel copied the SQE at submit time, buffer included
The submit fails with -EFAULT because stack buffers are rejected
Safe as long as the read hits the page cache
Undefined behaviour: the read may complete after the function returned and write into a dead stack frame
explain: The kernel copies the SQE, not the buffer it points to. If the read does not complete inline it finishes later and writes into memory that may now hold another function's locals. Even the page-cache case is not guaranteed to complete inline. Keep buffers alive until their CQE arrives.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototype pollution: one request changes every object
question: A code reviewer sees `target[k1][k2] = v` where `k1` and `k2` come from a JSON body. The team proposes rejecting only the key `__proto__`. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: __proto__ is the only way to reach Object.prototype
k1 = constructor and a deeper write via prototype still reach Object.prototype; refuse all three names or use own-key checks and null-prototype objects
JSON.parse already removes __proto__, so the check is redundant
The check must be case-insensitive because JavaScript property names ignore case
explain: MDN describes the constructor.prototype route explicitly, and our test showed it working even with --disable-proto=delete. JSON.parse keeps __proto__ as an own key rather than removing it, and property names are case-sensitive.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
question: Why is a 2-second regex match worse on a Node.js server than on a server that runs each request on its own thread?
options: Because V8 cannot run regular expressions on a worker thread
Because Node.js restarts the process whenever a regex exceeds one second
It is not worse: Node.js automatically moves regexes to the Worker Pool
Because Node.js runs every request's JavaScript on one Event Loop, so the match delays all other clients, not just the attacker
explain: Regex matching is ordinary JavaScript work on the Event Loop. The Worker Pool runs only specific I/O and CPU APIs. A thread-per-request server would lose one thread; a Node.js process loses all its JavaScript capacity for the duration.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Deserialisation in JavaScript: node-serialize to React2Shell
question: A team wants to send a 'job' object containing a callback function from one service to another and proposes node-serialize. What should they do instead?
options: Use node-serialize but strip the function marker with a regex
Use eval on the receiving side but inside a try/catch
Base64-encode the serialised object so it cannot be tampered with
Send only data (for example a job type name and JSON parameters), validate it with a schema, and map the type name to code the receiving service already contains
explain: Code should never travel as data across a trust boundary. An allowlist of job types mapped to local functions gives the same flexibility with no deserialisation of code. Regex stripping is a blocklist, try/catch does not stop code from running, and Base64 is an encoding, not protection.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
question: Which single change would have broken the Discord chain at the navigation step?
options: Raising the bug bounty
Turning nodeIntegration on
Adding the sandbox attribute to the embed iframes, so they cannot navigate the top-level window
Loading the embed over HTTP instead of HTTPS
explain: Both Discord's interim fix and Electron's advisory workaround were to sandbox iframes. Without the top-level navigation, the iframe's XSS stays inside the iframe, which has no access to the main window's built-ins or preload API.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: mimalloc: three free lists per page
question: A loop does `p = malloc(48); free(p);` a billion times on one thread. Without `local_free` (frees pushed straight onto `free`), what would mimalloc lose?
options: The guarantee that the slow path runs regularly, so remote frees and deferred work could wait forever
Correctness: blocks would be handed out twice
Locality, because blocks would come from other pages
Nothing; local_free exists only for debugging
explain: With one list, the same block is pushed and popped forever and free never empties, so malloc_generic never runs. thread_free would never be collected and deferred-free callbacks would never fire. local_free makes free run dry after a bounded number of allocations.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
question: A test with 5 client processes runs for 10 minutes and 40 writes end as info. Roughly how many operations can be concurrent near the end of the history?
options: At most 5, because there are only 5 processes
Exactly 40, the info writes alone
Zero, because the test is over
Up to about 45: the 5 live processes plus 40 writes that might still take effect
explain: Each info write stays open until the end of the history, and the crashed processes were replaced by fresh ones that keep issuing operations. So concurrency near the end is the live processes plus every unresolved info op, which is what makes checking expensive.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
question: You add one more knob to the matmul kernel: a vector width with 3 legal values. Everything else is unchanged. What happens to the 6000-configuration space?
options: It grows by 3 configurations, to 6003
It triples, to 18000 configurations
It stays at 6000 because vector width is derived from BLOCK_K
It grows only if you also add shapes to the key
explain: Knobs combine multiplicatively: every existing configuration is now three configurations, one per vector width. This is why autotuning is a search problem rather than a loop over a list, and why pruning matters before you compile anything.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
question: Why do people benchmark packet I/O with 64 byte frames rather than 1500 byte frames?
options: Because they maximize packets per second, so fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, syscalls, metadata) dominate and are exposed
Because 64 byte frames are the most common size on real networks
Because NICs can only DMA 64 bytes at a time
Because larger frames do not fit in a 2 KiB packet buffer
explain: Throughput in bits is the same, but small frames mean the most packets per second, and most driver and stack costs are per packet, not per byte. That is the worst case a data plane must survive.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
question: With SPDK's deferred-doorbell option on, a thread calls spdk_nvme_ns_cmd_read 16 times and then calls spdk_nvme_qpair_process_completions once. How many SQ tail doorbell writes did those 16 submissions need?
options: 0, NVMe needs no doorbell
explain: With the option set, submission only builds commands in the SQ ring; the doorbell is rung inside the poll call, once for everything submitted since the last poll.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
question: Using the Triton tutorial's count, what is the softmax speedup bound for M = N = 4096?
options: About 2x
About 3x
About 4x
About 8x
explain: Naive: (5MN + 2M) + (3MN + 2M) = 8MN + 4M element accesses. Fused: 2MN. Ratio (8MN + 4M) / 2MN = 4.0005 for M = N = 4096.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
question: Your loss uses F.kl_div(log_q, log_p, log_target=True, reduction="mean") on a batch of 32 examples over 1000 classes, then multiplies by T squared. Compared with the intended loss, the soft term is:
options: 1000 times too small, because mean divides by every element, not by the batch size
Correct as written
32 times too large
Equal to the cross-entropy instead of KL
explain: With reduction="mean" PyTorch averages over all 32 x 1000 elements. The KL per example is a sum over classes, so the mathematically correct reduction is batchmean (sum divided by 32). The soft term ends up 1000 times smaller and the hard loss silently dominates.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: On-policy distillation in code: student samples, teacher scores
question: A student fine-tuned on teacher-written answers does well on short replies but drifts into nonsense on long ones, while the teacher stays on track. Which change targets the cause most directly?
options: Raise the softmax temperature to 10
Switch from KL divergence to mean squared error on probabilities
Remove the hard-label loss
Train on the student's own sampled continuations with teacher token-level feedback (on-policy distillation)
explain: The symptom is compounding error from train-inference mismatch: the student never trained on its own imperfect prefixes. On-policy distillation (GKD, MiniLLM) samples from the student and asks the teacher what it should have done at each of those prefixes.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
question: You double the batch size and halve the context length per request. What happens to the total KV cache?
options: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
It grows 4x
explain: Total cache is proportional to batch x tokens per sequence. $2 \times 0.5 = 1$, so the cache is unchanged, though per-step attention work per sequence drops.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
question: Which statement about H2O is correct?
options: It needs the model to be fine-tuned
It scores tokens by attention they received in past steps, as a proxy for future importance
It keeps every token but at lower precision
It keeps only heavy hitters and no recent tokens
explain: H2O is training-free and uses local statistics: the sum of attention each token received so far. The paper finds this as effective as using future attention, and that keeping both heavy hitters and recent tokens is needed.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
question: Why can layer-wise loading start computing layer 0 before layers 1 to 31 of the cached KV have arrived?
options: Because attention at layer 0 only reads layer 0's keys and values
Because the GPU recomputes the missing layers in parallel
Because KV caches are stored layer-interleaved by token
Because the scheduler skips attention for cached tokens
explain: Each layer's attention uses only the K and V produced at that same layer. Layer 0 needs nothing from deeper layers, so it can run as soon as its own KV is in HBM while later layers are still in flight.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
question: Two events have Lamport timestamps L(x) = 5 and L(y) = 9. Which conclusion is valid?
options: x happened before y
y did not happen before x
x and y are concurrent
x happened about 4 ms before y
explain: If y happened before x, the Clock Condition would force L(y) < L(x), which is false. That is all you can conclude: x may have happened before y, or they may be concurrent. Lamport timestamps have no unit of time.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
question: The ColBERT paper reports that at re-ranking depth k = 10 the BERT-base cross-encoder needs about 180x more FLOPs than ColBERT, but at k = 1000 it needs 13,900x more. Why does the gap widen as k grows?
options: ColBERT skips most documents once k is large
The cross-encoder's cost grows with k (one transformer pass per document) while ColBERT's dominant cost, the single query encoding, does not
MaxSim becomes cheaper per document when k is large
BERT attention is quadratic in k
explain: The cross-encoder pays a full transformer pass over query plus document for each of the k candidates. ColBERT pays one query pass regardless of k, and the per-document MaxSim is tiny. Attention is quadratic in sequence length, not in k.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
question: BiPali and ColPali use the same PaliGemma backbone and training data, yet score 58.8 and 81.3 on ViDoRe. What is the difference between them?
options: ColPali runs OCR on the page first
BiPali averages the patch vectors into one vector per page; ColPali keeps one vector per patch and scores with MaxSim
ColPali uses a larger language model
BiPali only sees the page title
explain: The paper builds the model step by step. BiPali mean-pools the language model's patch outputs into a single dense vector. ColPali keeps every patch vector and uses late interaction, which is the 22.5-point jump.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
question: Why does Coconut, like iCoT, reset the optimizer state when the training stage changes?
options: To free GPU memory used by the KV cache
Because the loss suddenly changes, and Adam-style moment estimates from the old stage can produce badly scaled updates
Because the vocabulary changes when <bot> and <eot> are added
To force the model to forget the language reasoning steps
explain: Each stage is effectively a new task: some text targets disappear and new latent slots appear. iCoT found that without resets the accuracy collapsed and did not recover. Coconut follows iCoT and resets at stage switches.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
question: A leaf has min_err = -2,000 and max_err = +2,000, but 99% of its keys are predicted within 8 slots. Which search strategy is likely faster on average, and why?
options: Exponential search, because its cost follows the typical error (about 8) rather than the 4,001-slot worst case
Bounded binary search, because the window guarantees correctness
Neither: both cost log2 of the array size
Linear scan, because errors are small
explain: Bounded binary search over 4,001 slots needs about 12 probes for every key. Exponential search with an error of 8 needs about 1 + 2 log2(8) = 7. Since nearly all keys are close, the exponential strategy wins on average, which is the effect ALEX measured.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
question: What does learned sparse retrieval keep from BM25, and what does it replace?
options: Keeps the inverted index and dot-product style scoring, replaces hand-made term weights with learned ones that may include new terms
Keeps the dense embedding, replaces the ANN index
Keeps the BM25 formula, replaces the tokenizer
Keeps nothing; it is a re-ranker
explain: The index structure and term-at-a-time scoring (walking one query term's posting list at a time and adding up scores, lesson 3) stay. The weights now come from a transformer and can sit on vocabulary terms the text never used.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
question: Why must LTR training data be grouped by query rather than treated as one big table of rows?
options: Because gradient boosting needs equal-size groups
Because the model needs the query text as a feature
Because labels and metrics only compare documents for the same query, so pairs and NDCG must be formed within a group
Because rows from different queries have different numbers of features
explain: A label of 2 for one query is not comparable to a 2 for another. Pairwise losses only pair documents of the same query, and NDCG is computed per query and then averaged.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
question: Result Z was shown at a position with estimated propensity 0.2 and was clicked 30 times over the logged queries. What total IPS weight do those clicks contribute?
explain: Each click is weighted by 1 / 0.2 = 5, so 30 clicks count as 150. Clicks at rarely examined positions count more because they reveal relevance that is usually hidden.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting
question: A model reads a long code file, then a new unrelated file starts. Which mechanism lets a Gated DeltaNet head discard the old file's associations within a few tokens?
options: The delta rule with $\beta_t=1$
L2 normalization of keys
A small $\alpha_t$ at the boundary
The short convolution
explain: The delta rule only edits the direction of the current key, one association per token, so it cannot clear thousands of stale associations quickly. A small $\alpha_t$ scales the whole state toward zero at once.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: What a fixed state cannot do: recall limits and state tracking
question: A DeltaNet with $\beta_t\in(0,1)$, unit keys and a state of one million numbers is trained on parity of short strings and tested on 1,000-bit strings. What do you expect?
options: It succeeds, because one million numbers can store 1,000 bits
It succeeds only if keys are not normalized
It succeeds once the gate $\alpha_t$ is added
It fails at long lengths: every transition's eigenvalues lie in [0, 1], whatever the state size
explain: Parity needs a flip, an eigenvalue that is negative (or complex). Storage is not the problem. Adding a gate in (0, 1) keeps eigenvalues nonnegative; extending beta to (0, 2) is the fix.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
question: A service runs with umask 027 and creates a file, asking for mode 666. What mode does the file get?
explain: 666 AND NOT 027: the owner digit keeps 6, the group digit 6 loses write (2) to become 4, and the others digit 6 loses everything (7) to become 0. Result 640.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Services, systemd and cron: what runs without anyone logged in
question: What does `*/5 * * * *` in a crontab mean?
options: At 5 minutes past every hour
Every 5 hours
Every 5 minutes
On the 5th day of every month
explain: The first field is minutes; */5 means every value divisible by 5 within the range. All other fields are *, so the job runs every five minutes, every hour, every day.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
question: Which log sequence most strongly suggests a successful password-guessing attack?
options: Many Invalid user lines from many addresses, no Accepted lines
Several Failed password for deploy from one address, then Accepted password for deploy from the same address
Accepted publickey for alice from alice's usual address
One sudo line for alice restarting nginx
explain: Background scanning (many invalid users, no success) is routine. Repeated failures for a real account followed by success from the same source means a guess worked. Treat the account as compromised.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
question: What is the difference between the CIS Controls and a CIS Benchmark?
options: The Controls are a prioritised list of practices for a whole programme; a Benchmark gives configuration settings for one product version
They are two names for the same document
The Controls are for Windows, the Benchmarks for Linux
Benchmarks are paid; Controls are free
explain: CIS Controls v8.1 are programme-level Safeguards (inventory, access control, logging and so on). A Benchmark is product-specific configuration guidance, such as the Ubuntu 22.04 benchmark. Benchmark PDFs are free.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Kernel lockdown modes and sysctl baselines across a fleet
question: You ship /etc/sysctl.d/60-hardening.conf with kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1. A host reports 0. A package installed /usr/lib/sysctl.d/90-debug.conf setting it to 0. Why does the package win?
options: Files in /usr always beat files in /etc
The kernel ignores files in /etc/sysctl.d
All files are sorted by name across directories and the last one to set a key wins; 90-debug sorts after 60-hardening
ptrace_scope cannot be set from a file
explain: sysctl.d(5): files are sorted lexicographically regardless of directory, and the latest name wins for a repeated key. /etc only wins over a file with the same name. Rename yours to sort later or override 90-debug.conf by name.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts
question: A Falco rule condition ends with `and not proc.name in (backup_tools)`. An attacker copies their tool to /tmp/rsync and runs it. What happens?
options: Falco blocks the process
The rule still fires because Falco checks file hashes
If rsync is in backup_tools, the rule is skipped: proc.name is just the program name, which the attacker chose
Falco crashes
explain: Name-based allowlists match whatever name the process has. Prefer stronger fields where possible (proc.exepath, container image, parent), and accept that every exclusion is a potential hiding place.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Ebury, an SSH backdoor on 400,000 servers over 15 years
question: After confirming Ebury on a server, what does ESET recommend?
options: Delete the malicious library and reboot
Rotate only the root password
Reinstall completely and treat every credential and key that was on the server as compromised
Run the detection script daily from then on
explain: ESET says a complete reinstallation is necessary, without reusing keys or credentials from the server. Cleaning in place leaves the stolen credentials valid and other persistence possibly in place.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair
question: On a Bottlerocket node an attacker with code execution writes a new unit file to /etc/systemd/system. What happens at the next reboot?
options: It runs at boot as root
It is gone: /etc is a memory-backed filesystem rendered from API settings at each boot
The node refuses to boot
dm-verity deletes it immediately
explain: Bottlerocket documents a stateless tmpfs /etc whose files are generated from templates on every boot, so hand edits do not persist. dm-verity protects the root filesystem, not /etc.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Measuring judge agreement: confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa
question: In the toy, every disagreement is exactly one grade apart. Which statistic best reflects that the judge is never wildly wrong?
options: Quadratic-weighted kappa or interval alpha
Unweighted Cohen's kappa
Raw accuracy
The number of pairs
explain: Weighted kappa and interval alpha charge disagreements by squared distance, so many off-by-one errors cost little (0.786 and 0.790 here) while unweighted kappa treats them as full misses (0.333). Report both: the unweighted one tells you how often grades match exactly.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Why open-ended output is hard to score
question: A metric correlates poorly with human ratings of single responses but orders five systems the same way humans do. How should you use it?
options: Use it to flag individual bad responses in production
Never use it for anything
Use it, with care, to compare whole systems on a test set, not to judge single outputs
Use it only on outputs shorter than the reference
explain: Novikova et al. found the same pattern: metrics are more reliable at the system level than at the segment level, because averaging over many outputs cancels some per-output errors.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Designing human evaluations and measuring agreement
question: In the toy, 5 of 7 disagreements involve the tie label. Which change most directly targets that?
options: Hire annotators who never use ties
Write an explicit tie rule with examples, run a calibration round, then re-measure kappa on a fresh overlap sample
Drop all pairs that any annotator called a tie, then report kappa on the rest
Switch to a 1 to 10 scale
explain: The disagreement is about what a tie means, which is a guideline problem. Dropping ties after the fact inflates agreement and biases the win rate; forbidding ties forces random picks on truly equal pairs.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Classifier guards: Llama Guard and NeMo Guardrails rails
question: Your agent reads emails and calls a refund tool. In NeMo Guardrails terms, which rail type is the most direct place to check that a refund call's arguments are allowed?
options: Input rails
Dialog rails
Execution rails
Output rails
explain: Execution rails control tool calls, their arguments and their results. Input and output rails see the user message and final response, not the tool call itself.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
question: Why does selective batching split the batch for attention but not for the QKV projection?
options: Attention has no weights, so batching it gains nothing and it must be skipped
The QKV projection runs on the CPU
Splitting the projection would require padding, splitting attention does not
Each token's projection uses only that token's row, but attention must combine a token only with earlier tokens of its own request
explain: A linear layer computes each output row from one input row, so the request a row belongs to is irrelevant and all rows share one weight read. Attention mixes rows, and mixing rows from different requests would be wrong, so it needs the boundaries (and each request's own past keys and values).

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
question: Which statement about the three engines is accurate according to their documentation?
options: All three swap preempted KV caches to CPU memory by default
SGLang keeps every running request's full max_new_tokens reserved until it finishes
vLLM V1 runs prefill and decode in separate scheduler queues with separate budgets
TensorRT-LLM's default capacity policy never pauses a request once started, while vLLM V1 recomputes preempted requests
explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT is TensorRT-LLM's default and guarantees started requests are not paused; vLLM V1 recomputes by default and removed CPU swapping for preemption. SGLang counts running requests' remaining tokens at an estimated ratio rather than their full maximum, and vLLM V1 uses one unified token budget.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
question: Why does the Outlines index map FSM states, rather than generated prefixes, to allowed tokens?
options: Prefixes are too short to be useful keys
There are finitely many states, each summarizing all prefixes that lead to it, so the table can be built once ahead of time
States are faster to hash than strings
The model's logits depend only on the FSM state
explain: Possible prefixes are unbounded, but the FSM has a fixed number of states, and any two prefixes that reach the same state allow exactly the same continuations. That is what makes ahead-of-time indexing possible. The logits still depend on the full prefix.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Ambiguity, negation and graceful fallback
question: Which parse is correct for *backend people who know java (not javascript) in hamburg*?
options: skills: [java], skills_not: [javascript]
skills: [java, javascript], skills_not: []
skills: [], skills_not: [java, javascript]
skills: [java], skills_not: [], text: not javascript
explain: Java is required and JavaScript is excluded. Option two is the dropped-negation error that appears in the lesson 5 set. Putting the exclusion in text makes it a scored match, which would actually boost profiles that mention JavaScript.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
question: PRP all-pairs at k=100 issues how many prompts, counting both orders?
explain: k(k-1) = 100 x 99 = 9,900: every unordered pair (4,950) in both orders.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
question: RankZephyr is distilled into 7B from GPT-4 orderings. Which cost quantity does distillation change?
options: The number of windows per query
The input tokens per window
The compute per token, plus access to batching, caching and logits when self-hosted
The number of output tokens per window
explain: Calls and tokens follow from k, w, s and L. Distillation shrinks the model, so each token costs less compute, and hosting it yourself unlocks the serving levers.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Listwise permutation generation with sliding windows
question: Which change most directly reduces the number of listwise calls for 100 candidates?
options: Shrinking the window from 20 to 10 at the same step of 10
Raising the step from 10 to 15 with w = 20 (overlap 5)
Running a second pass
Adding more few-shot examples
explain: Calls per pass are the floor of (M - w) divided by s, plus 1. With s = 15: floor(80/15) + 1 = 6 instead of 9. The cost is a smaller overlap (only the best 5 passages are carried along), and since 15 does not divide 80, the last window covers ranks 6 to 25 and ranks 1 to 5 are never reranked. Shrinking w to 10 with s = 10 removes the overlap entirely, so passages could no longer travel between windows.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Cascades: answer cheaply, score the answer, escalate if unsure
question: Which workload is the best fit for a cascade rather than a router?
options: A voice assistant with a 300 ms latency budget
A chat product where most answers are long essays
A nightly batch that labels support tickets into 12 categories, where a wrong label is cheap to detect
Any workload, because cascades are always more accurate
explain: Short answers make the wasted weak call cheap, a batch job does not care about the extra latency, and an easy correctness check makes the scorer reliable. A tight latency budget punishes escalation, and long answers make the wasted weak generation expensive.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
question: You switch a working SIFT pipeline to ORB but leave `cv.BFMatcher()` with its default arguments. What is the most likely result?
options: It works the same, since all descriptors are vectors
Matches are much worse, because the default L2 norm treats bit strings as numbers
It throws an error because ORB has no descriptors
It becomes faster and more accurate
explain: BFMatcher defaults to NORM_L2, which is right for SIFT. ORB descriptors are packed bits, and L2 on the byte values does not measure how many tests disagree. Pass cv.NORM_HAMMING.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
question: Why should `compare_exchange_weak` be used inside a loop?
options: It may fail spuriously even when the value matched, so the caller must be ready to retry
It is slower than the strong version and loops hide the cost
It never updates `expected`, so the loop must reload
It only works on x86
explain: cppreference: the weak form may act as if the comparison failed even when it succeeded, for example when a store-conditional loses its reservation. Inside a retry loop that is harmless, and on LL/SC machines it can be faster. It does update `expected` on failure.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
question: In the hazard pointer protocol, why must a reader re-read the shared pointer after publishing its hazard pointer?
options: To refresh the CPU cache
Because the node may have been removed and retired between the first load and the publication, and a scan that ran in between would not have seen the hazard
To implement the ABA tag
It is optional; publishing is enough
explain: Michael's condition is that the hazard pointer must have pointed to the node continuously from a time when the node was still reachable. Re-reading proves the node was still in the structure after the hazard became visible, so any later scan will see it.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
question: You parse 2,000 lines. The ground truth has 40 templates. Your parser emits 60 templates, of which 30 group their messages exactly as the ground truth does. What are RGA and PGA?
options: RGA = 40/60 = 0.67 and PGA = 1.0, because every ground-truth template was covered
explain: Recall divides the correct templates by the ground-truth count (30/40 = 0.75) and precision divides by what the parser produced (30/60 = 0.50). Their harmonic mean is 2 x 0.75 x 0.50 / 1.25 = 0.60. Emitting too many templates, which is what over-partitioning does, is punished by precision; merging templates is punished by recall.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Log formats: syslog, JSON and Windows XML
question: Two data centres, in London and Chicago, send RFC 3164 syslog to one collector. Why is ordering their events by timestamp unreliable?
options: RFC 3164 timestamps are in seconds, not milliseconds
UDP reorders packets by priority
Syslog sorts messages by PRI, not time
RFC 3164 timestamps carry no time zone (and no year), so 09:14 in Chicago and 09:14 in London look identical
explain: Without a zone, the collector has to guess each sender's offset. RFC 5424 fixes this by requiring RFC 3339 timestamps with an offset or Z. Lesson 6 shows what a wrong guess does to an investigation.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: SIEM queries: SQL, KQL and SPL on one toy dataset
question: In KQL, why does `where FileName == "powershell.exe"` risk missing real events?
options: == does not work on strings
It only matches the first row
FileName is not a column of DeviceProcessEvents
== is case-sensitive, and Windows file names can appear as PowerShell.EXE
explain: Windows treats file names case-insensitively, so attackers and legitimate tools can produce any capitalisation. Use =~ (case-insensitive equals) for such fields.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Detection as code: rules in git, tests and CI
question: A colleague edits the rule to fix noise and the unit tests still pass. What can you conclude?
options: The rule is now correct
The SIEM will convert it correctly
The rule has no false positives
The rule still gives the expected answer on the cases in the test file, and nothing more
explain: Tests prove behaviour only on the cases they contain. That is why every miss and every false positive should be added as a new case, and why lab emulation (lesson 17) checks real event shapes.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
question: Which detection causes the attacker the most pain to evade, according to the Pyramid of Pain?
options: Alerting whenever an Office application spawns a command interpreter
Blocking their command-and-control IP address
Blocking the SHA-256 hash of their loader
Blocking their phishing domain
explain: Office spawning a shell is a behaviour (a TTP). Changing a hash, IP or domain is cheap; changing how the intrusion starts means new tradecraft.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
question: With Ring Attention on N hosts, after how many compute steps has host 0's query block seen every KV block of the sequence (one layer, forward pass)?
options: N
log2 N
N squared
explain: Each step delivers one new KV block from the predecessor. Host 0 starts with its own block and needs N - 1 more hops, so N compute steps in total (Algorithm 1 loops over the N - 1 transfers).

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
question: A position's halting unit outputs 0.3, 0.5, 0.4 at steps 1 to 3, with epsilon = 0.01. When does it halt and what is its remainder?
options: Step 2, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.4
It never halts because the sum never equals exactly 0.99
explain: Running sums are 0.3, 0.8, 1.2. The first to reach 0.99 is step 3, so N = 3. The remainder is 1 minus the sum before the halting step: 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. The step-3 halting probability (0.4) is replaced by the remainder so the weights sum to 1.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
question: During training your recurrent-depth model logs validation loss 0.81 at r = 1 and 0.80 at r = 32, and the gap has not grown for thousands of steps; mean cosine similarity between states is a steady 0.3. What is the most likely problem?
options: The learning rate is too low, so both losses fall slowly
Representation collapse: all token states have become identical
The model has learned to ignore its recurrent state, so extra iterations do nothing
Nothing; equal losses mean the loop has converged
explain: Equal loss at 1 and 32 iterations means the core's output does not depend on how many times it ran: the model solved what it could without the loop. That was Huginn's second failed run and our step-signal variant. Collapse shows up in the cosine-similarity monitor instead; converged loops still differ sharply between r = 1 and r = 32.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
question: You fine-tune a 7B model with Adam but freeze all but 1% of its weights. Which part of the 107.8 GB shrinks the most?
options: The 16-bit copy of the frozen weights, because frozen weights are not loaded
Nothing changes, because Adam allocates state for every weight in the model
Gradients and Adam states, because they are only needed for trainable weights
Activations, because a frozen layer does not store activations
explain: Frozen weights still have to sit in memory for the forward pass, and activations are still needed to backpropagate into trainable parts. But gradients and the three fp32 optimizer tensors exist only for trainable parameters, so 14 of the 16 bytes per parameter disappear for the frozen 99%.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
question: A team wants to teach Llama-2-7B a new programming language by training on 20B tokens of raw source code, and to keep its English skills. What does the evidence suggest?
options: LoRA at r = 16 will match full fine-tuning and forget nothing
Full fine-tuning will likely learn the domain better, while LoRA preserves more of the base skills; pick based on which matters more
Prompt tuning is the best choice because it has the fewest parameters
Rank does not matter in continued pretraining
explain: In Biderman et al.'s continued pretraining runs, full fine-tuning outperformed every LoRA rank on the target domain, and LoRA forgot less. That is a real tradeoff, not a free lunch, and rank clearly ordered LoRA's results.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff
question: Your unlearned model gets a TOFU forget quality (KS-test p-value) of 0.0004. What does that mean?
options: The model forgot 99.96% of the forget set
The model's utility is 0.0004
The model is statistically indistinguishable from the retain model
The truth-ratio distribution on the forget set is very unlikely to come from the same distribution as the retain model's, so unlearning is incomplete or overshot
explain: Forget quality is the p-value of a two-sample KS test between the unlearned and retain models' truth-ratio distributions. A tiny p-value means the distributions clearly differ, which is poor unlearning in either direction. It is not a percentage of facts forgotten.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: A safe analysis lab and the analysis workflow
question: Why use a simulated internet (INetSim, FakeNet-NG) instead of no network at all?
options: It makes the malware run faster
It is required by law
The sample often reveals its domains and protocols only when something answers, and nothing real is reached
It hides the analysis VM from the malware
explain: With no network, many samples stall at their first lookup. A fake service answers, so you capture the domains, URLs and protocol the sample uses, while nothing leaves the lab.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Disassemblers and decompilers: from bytes back to C
question: A decompiler shows `if (local_14 < 0x5a)` but you suspect a signed versus unsigned mistake matters for a size check. What should you do?
options: Trust the decompiler; it is always exact
Rename local_14 and move on
Check the conditional jump in the disassembly: jl or jg mean signed, jb or ja mean unsigned
Rerun the decompiler with a different font
explain: The jump instruction is the ground truth for signedness. Decompilers guess types; when the detail matters, confirm in assembly.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
question: Why did notes.txt not match, even though it contains both the banner and the URL?
options: YARA cannot read .txt files
The condition requires uint16(0) == 0x5A4D, and the text file does not start with MZ
The filesize was too large
nocase only works on PE files
explain: The condition combines file structure and content. A text file that quotes the strings fails the structural check, which is exactly the false positive the check was added to prevent.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard
question: With a Matryoshka model you shortlist with 2-d prefixes and keep the top 3 documents. In the toy, which statement is true?
options: The shortlist is B, A, C, so the true best match A survives, and the 8-d rerank puts A first
The shortlist is A, B, C in exact final order, so no rerank is needed
The shortlist is C, B, A, so A is lost
A 2-d prefix cannot be used for search at all
explain: At m = 2 the Matryoshka scores are B 1.000, A 1.000, C 0.998: the right documents, in blurred order. Reranking those three at m = 8 gives A 0.997, B 0.757, C 0.616. A shortlist needs to contain the right items, not order them perfectly.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
question: Why did Megatron adopt 1F1B (PipeDream-Flush) over GPipe even though both have the same bubble?
options: 1F1B needs no pipeline flush
1F1B sends fewer bytes between stages
1F1B caps in-flight microbatches at p instead of m, so activation memory stops growing with the number of microbatches
1F1B lets each microbatch use slightly stale weights, which is faster
explain: The bubble is (p-1)/m for both. GPipe stores activations for all m microbatches; 1F1B starts backward passes early and never has more than p outstanding. This is what makes a large m (small bubble) affordable.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Virtual addresses, page tables and the DTB, walked by hand
question: In the PAE split, why are the PD and PT indices 9 bits each?
options: Because Windows reserves 3 bits of every address
Each table is a 4 KB page holding 8-byte entries, so it has 512 entries, and 512 = 2^9
Because PAE pages are 9 KB
Because 9 bits is the size of a PID
explain: 4096 bytes per table divided by 8 bytes per entry gives 512 entries, and choosing one of 512 needs exactly 9 bits.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Finding processes: walking the list versus scanning for tags
question: Why does walking ActiveProcessLinks require subtracting 0xB8 from each Flink?
options: Because Windows encrypts pointers with 0xB8
Each Flink points to the links field inside the next EPROCESS, which sits 0xB8 bytes after the start of that structure
Because 0xB8 is the size of a page header
Because PIDs are stored 0xB8 bytes before each list
explain: Embedded list entries point at each other, not at the structures that contain them. To reach the structure's other fields you step back by the offset of the links field.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Handles, mutexes, sockets and registry hives in memory
question: Why might a registry value found in memory differ from the same value in the hive file on disk?
options: The disk version is always encrypted
Changes are held in memory and written to the hive file later, so memory can hold newer values
Registry hives are never loaded into memory
Memory stores only deleted keys
explain: The loaded hive in kernel memory is the live copy. The file on disk is updated when the system flushes, so recent changes may exist only in RAM.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Timelines from memory: what carries a time, and merging it
question: Why must you deduplicate and filter timeliner output before reading it?
options: Several plugins report the same objects and some report several times per object, so raw rows overstate and repeat events
Because timeliner output is encrypted
Because duplicates mean the image is corrupt
Because body files cannot be sorted
explain: pslist and psscan both list every process, and in Volatility 3 2.28.2 timeliner also prints earlier rows again after each later plugin: PsList gave 476 rows for 34 processes in a full run, 34 when run alone. Group by object and keep the source plugin.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
question: A team patches their allocator from 4 to 8 classes per doubling. Which outcome should they expect?
options: Total memory always falls by about 9%
External fragmentation disappears because rounding is smaller
Allocation becomes slower because each request must search all classes
Worst-case internal waste falls from about 20% to about 11%, with more partly empty slabs to offset part of the gain
explain: Worst-case waste is just under 1/(n+1): 20% for n = 4, 11% for n = 8. But twice as many classes means twice as many places for partly filled slabs and cached objects to sit, so the net saving depends on the workload. Class lookup stays a computation, not a search.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
question: Ten threads each run `counter.fetch_add(1, Relaxed)` 1000 times; then main joins all ten and reads the counter. What does main see?
options: Exactly 10000
Any value from 1000 to 10000, since Relaxed does not order the increments
10000 on x86 but possibly less on ARM64
Undefined behavior, because Relaxed operations race
explain: Each fetch_add is atomic, so none are lost, and all of them sit in one modification order. Joining a thread creates happens-before from everything it did to the code after the join, so main reads the final value. Relaxed is not a race: races need a non-atomic access.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
question: A shutdown flag is set by one thread and polled by workers, which simply exit their loop when they see it. No other data is passed through the flag. Which ordering fits?
options: SeqCst, to make sure workers see it quickly
Release store and Acquire load
Relaxed
AcqRel on both store and load
explain: The flag carries no other data, so no happens-before edge is needed: Relaxed gives atomicity, and the model says nothing about speed anyway. If the workers had to read results or config written before the flag, you would upgrade to Release and Acquire. AcqRel is only for read-modify-write operations.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
question: CPU 1 calls synchronize_rcu() at time 10. Reader X started at time 8 and ends at 12; reader Y starts at 11 and ends at 30. Ignoring batching delays, when may synchronize_rcu() return?
options: At 30, after both readers
At 12, after X; Y need not be waited for
At 10, immediately, because readers take no locks
At 11, when Y starts
explain: Only pre-existing read-side critical sections count. X was running at time 10, so the grace period must cover it. Y started after the removal and cannot have obtained the removed pointer, so waiting for it would be wasted. Real implementations may return somewhat later because they batch requests.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Stack buffer overflow: when a copy runs past the end
question: Which change fixes `strcpy(buf, name)` for `char buf[8]` without silently corrupting memory for long names?
options: Make buf 64 bytes so normal names fit
Call strcpy twice to check the result
Use strncpy(buf, name, sizeof buf) and nothing else
Use snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "%s", name), or reject names with strlen(name) >= sizeof buf
explain: A bigger buffer only raises the bar: a 65-byte name still overflows. strncpy stops at the size but leaves buf unterminated for long names, so the next read runs off the end. snprintf truncates and terminates; an explicit length check rejects the input.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Integer overflow and signedness: when the size math lies
question: Code does `uint32_t n = w * h * 4; char *px = malloc(n);` for an image of width w and height h from a file, then writes w*h*4 bytes. What is the bug?
options: None: malloc checks the size
The bug is only that malloc's result is not checked
malloc can't allocate images
w * h * 4 can wrap in 32 bits, so px is smaller than the bytes later written
explain: For a large enough w and h the product exceeds 4,294,967,295 and wraps, so the allocation is small. The later writes use the true size and overflow. Checking malloc's result for NULL does not help because malloc succeeds. Fix: check each multiplication (calloc or __builtin_mul_overflow) and limit w and h.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Finding memory bugs: warnings, sanitizers, Valgrind and fuzzing
question: Why is AddressSanitizer usually not enabled in production builds?
options: It only works on Windows
Its documentation says the runtime is a testing tool not designed for security-sensitive production use, and it costs about 2x speed and more memory
It produces many false alarms
It removes bounds checks
explain: ASan is precise (its docs say no false alarms) but slows programs about 2x, uses extra memory, and its runtime was not built with production security constraints in mind. It belongs in testing, CI (continuous integration: the build and tests that run on every change) and fuzzing.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
question: You switch from batch hard to batch all without changing anything else and validation mAP drops. Which change would most directly test the 'washed out' explanation?
options: Increase the margin to 1.0
Average the loss only over triplets with non-zero loss
Square the distances
Use K = 1
explain: If zero-loss triplets dilute the gradient, averaging only the active terms removes the dilution. Hermans and colleagues ran this test and the non-zero average performed much better than the plain average.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
question: A new hash map is 2x faster than the old one in a benchmark with 1000 keys, but the service using 50 million keys sees no gain. What is the most plausible reason?
options: At 1000 keys both maps fit in cache, so the benchmark measured hashing and probing on hot data; at 50 million keys both are dominated by cache misses to DRAM
The benchmark forgot DoNotOptimize
The service has more threads
Hash maps are O(1), so size cannot matter
explain: A small key set keeps the whole table in L1 or L2, where instruction counts dominate. A huge table makes nearly every probe a DRAM miss, and a design that saves instructions but makes as many misses gains little. Big-O hides exactly this constant. Sweep the size before trusting the 2x.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Fully async RL: busy engines, paid for in staleness
question: An agentic batch has 8 trajectories per group; one takes 40 turns while the rest finish in 3. Which setting keeps engine slots busiest while that trajectory runs?
options: --rollout-submission-granularity group, so the group stays together
--pause-generation-mode abort, to kill stragglers
--update-weights-interval 0
--rollout-submission-granularity sample, so each finished trajectory frees its own slot
explain: With sample granularity, the seven short trajectories free their slots as soon as they finish, and new groups start in them. With group granularity, all eight slots stay reserved until the 40-turn trajectory returns. Abort mode is rejected under fully async.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
question: A 3-slot cache holds X, Y and Z. Their next requests are: X in 7 requests, Y never, Z in 2 requests. A miss for W arrives. What does Belady's MIN evict?
options: Z, because it was used least recently
X, because it is needed later than Z
Y, because it is never requested again
W is not admitted, because MIN only evicts on hits
explain: MIN evicts the object whose next request is furthest away, and never counts as furthest of all. Recency (option one) is LRU's rule, not MIN's. X is a reasonable second choice but loses to Y.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
question: Using Lykouris and Vassilvitskii's result, what happens to their predictor-augmented Marker algorithm if the oracle's predictions become arbitrarily bad?
options: It stays within O(log k) of optimal, the same bound as classic Marker without predictions
Its competitive ratio grows without bound
It becomes exactly as good as Belady's MIN
It refuses to evict
explain: The point of the construction is robustness: the ratio improves as prediction error falls, but it is always capped by O(log k), which is achievable with no oracle at all. Blindly following the oracle has no such cap.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: a test device, a proxy and the app's own files
question: In the Starbucks case, the app kept its OAuth token in the Keychain, yet the password still leaked. Which MASVS control did the app fail?
options: MASVS-STORAGE-2: the app prevents leakage of sensitive data, here through a log file
MASVS-NETWORK-1, because the password was sent in cleartext
MASVS-RESILIENCE-1, because the phone could be jailbroken
MASVS-CRYPTO-1, because the Keychain is weak
explain: Storing the token securely satisfies part of STORAGE-1, but the password reached a log through the crash reporter: a leak, which is STORAGE-2. There was no network flaw in the advisory, and resilience controls would not stop an app from writing its own log.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code
question: An app's WebView exposes `addJavascriptInterface(Bridge(), 'native')` and loads only `https://help.example.com`. The help site embeds a third-party chat widget in an iframe. What can the widget's script do?
options: Call the bridge's @JavascriptInterface methods, because the object is injected into every frame, including iframes
Nothing: iframes cannot see objects added by the app
Only read the page's text
Call the bridge only if the user taps inside the iframe
explain: Android's guidance says addJavascriptInterface injects the object into every frame, including iframes, with no way to check the calling frame's origin. Third-party content on your own page therefore reaches your native code. addWebMessageListener with origin rules, or no bridge, fixes it.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Running a mobile app assessment end to end, and where to practise
question: The scope says 'profile MAS-L2+P'. During testing you find the app has no jailbreak detection and no obfuscation. How should these appear in the report?
options: As informational observations at most, since MAS-R is not in the agreed profile and their absence is not in itself a vulnerability
As high-severity findings under MASVS-STORAGE
They should not be mentioned at all
As critical, because the backend can be called directly
explain: Resilience controls belong to MAS-R. Under L2+P they are optional defence in depth, so at most an observation, perhaps with a note on when they would matter (fraud, cheating). Calling the API directly is a backend question, answered by server-side checks, not by client obfuscation.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Decoupled RoPE: why position breaks absorption
question: A colleague's absorbed MLA decoder applies RoPE at position t to the full 512-wide absorbed query, then dots it with the cached latents. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, RoPE commutes with the latent projection
It only fails for contexts longer than 4K
The rotation now acts in latent space, which does not equal rotating each head's keys; position information is wrong and the scores no longer match the trained model
The cache size doubles
explain: RoPE in MLA must only touch the decoupled 64-wide parts. The content part was trained without rotation, and a rotation applied in the 512-wide latent space is not the per-head offset rotation $R_{j-t}$ of the key, so the scores no longer match the trained model. Lesson 5 runs this exact bug.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why MLA can beat GQA at equal cache, and converting models
question: A GQA layer like those in Meta's Llama models has 32 query heads, 8 KV heads and $d_h = 128$. What latent size rewrites it exactly as MLA, and what happens to its cache?
options: 128, and the cache shrinks 16x
4,096, and the cache doubles
1,024, and the cache halves
2,048, and the cache stays the same size
explain: The latent is the stacked keys and values, $2 g d_h = 2 \times 8 \times 128 = 2048$, which is exactly what GQA already caches per token per layer. Saving memory needs a further compression step.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
question: Using the simplified bandwidth model, which change most reduces the extra bytes read per step when 32 distinct adapters share each batch?
options: Raising the batch size to 64
Sorting rows by adapter
Using more prefill tokens per batch
Halving every adapter's rank
explain: Extra traffic is proportional to (distinct adapters) x rank. Halving the rank halves it. Sorting is required for SGMV to work but does not change how many adapter bytes must be read, and a bigger batch with more tenants can add distinct adapters.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
question: A LangChain `MultiQueryRetriever` with defaults is called through `invoke` over a base retriever with k = 5. What comes back?
options: The 5 highest RRF-scored documents
Up to 15 unique documents from the 3 rewrites, in the order they were retrieved
Exactly 20 documents including duplicates
Only the documents that appear in all 3 lists
explain: With include_original=False, 3 rewrites are searched (sequentially on the sync path) and the unique union is returned, up to 3 x 5 = 15 documents, in query order. There is no rank fusion and no truncation to k.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
question: Why does the pipeline run duoBERT on monoBERT's top 50 instead of directly on BM25's top 1000?
options: duoBERT cannot read passages that BM25 retrieved
Pairwise scoring grows as k(k-1): 1000 candidates would need 999,000 inferences instead of 2450
duoBERT is less accurate than monoBERT, so it should see fewer documents
BM25 scores must be normalized before a pairwise model can use them
explain: Pairwise cost is quadratic in the list length. On 1000 candidates, duoBERT would need 1000 x 999 = 999,000 inferences per query, about 290 times the 3450 that monoBERT plus duoBERT on 50 use. Putting the quadratic model last, on a short list, is exactly the cascade idea.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: Why does Margin-MSE train the student on score margins instead of making it reproduce the teacher's raw scores?
options: Different architectures naturally produce scores on different scales; only the ordering matters, and the margin preserves it
Raw scores are not available from cross-encoders
Margins are cheaper to compute at query time
MSE cannot be applied to raw scores
explain: A dot-product bi-encoder or ColBERT produces scores on a very different scale from a cross-encoder. Forcing the same raw values fights the architecture. Ranking only needs the student to separate relevant from non-relevant by the same amount, which is what the margin captures.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain
question: At depth k = 2 in DeepSeek-V3's scheme, which inputs does the module use for position i, and which token does it predict?
options: h_i from the main model and Emb(t_i+1); predicts t_i+2
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+3); predicts t_i+3
Only Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
explain: Depth k combines h at depth k - 1 with the embedding of t(i+k) and predicts t(i+k+1). For k = 2 that is h from depth 1, Emb(t(i+2)), and target t(i+3).

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
question: You serve a Gloeckle-style 4-token model with greedy decoding and enable self-speculative decoding with all 4 heads. What happens to the generated text?
options: It becomes more diverse because heads 2 to 4 inject their own choices
It is identical to greedy decoding with head 1; only the number of forward passes drops
It is identical only if every draft is accepted
It degrades slightly, which is the price of a 3x speedup
explain: Every emitted token is one that head 1 would have chosen given the same prefix: drafts are kept only when they match head 1's prediction, and the first mismatch is replaced by head 1's token. Acceptance rate changes speed, never content.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
